chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ABSTRACT
chunks.content:
ABSTRACT
Problem solving styles are critical dimensions in corporate decision making. In order to study
the comparative problem-solving styles of college graduate students majoring in information
systems versus business administration, the Kirton Adaption-Innovation Inventory (KAI)
was used to determine the cognitive styles of the students enrolled in the Master of Science
in Information Systems (MSIS) and the Master of Business Administration (MBA) programs
at the University of Mary-Hardin Baylor (UMHB) during the spring semester of 2007. The
results of the study were also analyzed by demographic variants.
i ntroduction
Dr. Michael J. Kirton, an eminent British organizational psychologist, developed a theory on
the assumption that all people solve problems and are creative, since both activities are the
results of the same brain function. His theory is well established and has been highly vali-
dated [Kirton, 1976; Kirton, 1994; Kirton, 1998]. A distinction is made between the level and
style of problem solving and creativity. Cognitive level, not measured by the Kirton Adaptive-
Inventory (A-I) Inventory [Kirton, 1998], refers to an individual’s inherent potential capacity,
such as intelligence. Cognitive style, measured by the Kirton A-I Inventory, is defined as
the “strategic, stable, characteristic, preferred manner in which people respond and seek to
bring about change.”
A study, utilizing the Kirton A-I Inventory that compared the problem-solving style, in terms
of adaption and innovation, of Information and Computer Science majors was conducted
by [Sim, E. R. and Wright, G., 2002]. This study concluded that there is no difference in
programming styles between information systems and computer science students as measured
by the Kirton’s A-I Inventory. The study did conclude, however, there was a gender differ-
ence in the Kirton A-I Inventory scores; women scored slightly more adaptively then men.
Appendix c n n n 715
[Kaufmann, G., Isaken, S. G., and Lauer, K., 1996] developed a regression plane showing the
distribution of Kirton A-I Inventory scores across managerial levels by gender. These authors
found a striking gender difference when observing Kirton A-I Inventory scores for males
and females analyzed across managerial levels. Males were found to be more innovatively
inclined than females at the lowest managerial level, whereas females obtained almost a full
standard deviation higher innovator score at the top, executive level of leadership.
Cognitive style differences, as measured by the Kirton A-I Inventory, lie on a continuum and
range from strong adaption to strong innovation. For large general populations, the distribu-
tion of scores forms a normal curve. Smaller groups can be predictably different from gen-
eral populations, depending on their problem-solving orientation, and may exhibit skewed

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ABSTRACT
chunks.content:
distributions about different means.
Adaptors prefer to operate with more structure than do innovators. Innovators prefer solving
problems by “thinking outside of the box”. Adaptors approach problems from within the given
frame of reference and strive to produce solutions that are “better” rather than “different.”
Adaptors are valued in a business environment since they tend to be the system experts and
are dedicated to its maintenance and efficiency. Adaptors are especially good at fine-tuning the
current rules and procedures in order to make them operate as effectively as possible. Innova-
tors, on the other hand, tend to detach a given problem from the customary frame of reference
and search for solutions that are typically seen as “different.” In summary, adaptors prefer to
solve problems using the rules and innovators tend to solve problems despite the rules.
During the stages of problem solving, innovators and adaptors have distinct patterns of behavior
as a result of their distinct cognitive styles. Adaptors generally accept problems as they have been
defined, including agreed-upon constraints. During data collection, they tend to exhaustively
collect and favor information and perspectives that are closely related to the original problem
structure. When generating ideas, adaptors prefer to generate only a few novel and creative solu-
tions that are relevant, readily-acceptable, and aimed at improving the current situation. Such
solutions are often easy to implement, which is not necessarily the case for solutions obtained by
innovators. Adaptors look for a quick resolution to problems, which leads to increased efficiency.
Innovators tend to reject the original and accepted definition of a problem. Instead, the
innovators will redefine the problem. Sometimes, on project teams, this leads to a break-
down in communication. In collecting data, innovators tend to look outside the original prob-
lem structure for different perspectives. During the generation of ideas, innovators generally
produce numerous novel and creative ideas, and some of these ideas are view as acceptable
by others. When evaluating and implementing solutions, innovators are less concerned with
immediate efficiency and potential disruption of their project team, and therefore tend to
look ahead to potential long-term gains [Kirton, 1994].
During problem definition, an adaptor’s chief aim is to define the problem as explicitly as pos-
sible in a way that is acceptable to authority, and hopefully to other members of their project
team. If a problem definition is supplied at the beginning of a project, adaptors will accept
this definition as fixed, clarify any questions that are not well-defined, and move forward to
a quick solution. Any ambiguity in the problem definition will cause the adaptor to become

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ABSTRACT
chunks.content:
frustrated and moving forward becomes difficult. Innovators approach the problem with
some freedom to explore different problem formulations. They delight in defining and rede-
fining, even when a problem statement is supplied [Isaksen, S. G. and Kaufmann, G., 1990].
716 n n n A ppendix c
Application
The Kirton A-I Inventory [Kirton, 1998] was introduced in 1976 and measures preferred
thinking. Respondents answer 32 questions that focus on how easy or difficult it is for a per-
son to present himself consistently, over a long period of time, in particular ways {refer to
Appendix A}. Each answer is assigned a value using a 5-point scale. The inventory is easily
understood and can be completed in less than 15 minutes. A person’s overall Kirton A-I score
will fall between 32 and 160, with a score of 32 representing the theoretical limit of highest
adaption, and a score of 160 representing the theoretical limit of highest innovation. In prac-
tice, scores typically fall between 40 and 150. For large general populations the distribution of
scores forms a normal curve with a theoretical mean of 96. In the United States, the observed
mean for the general population is 95, while the observed mean for both U.S. engineers and
managers (measured separately) is 97 [Kirton, 1998]. Table C-1 displays the categories of
adaptors and innovators for the theoretical distribution of Kirton A-I Inventory scores:
Table c-1 Kirton A-I Inventory Score Categories.
i nnovators Adaptors
96–110 Mild 95–80
111–124 Medium 79–65
125–139 High 64–50
140 or more Very High 49 or less
It is important to note that high scores are not “good” and low scores are not “bad”; it is the
relative difference between the scores of the two individuals or between an individual and
the mean of a group that is important. In general, a difference of 10 points between indi-
viduals is noticeable over time. A difference of 20 points or more can lead to difficulties in
communication and may require considerable coping behavior [Kirton, 1998].
The Kirton A-I Inventory was administered to graduate students enrolled in both the Master
of Science in Information Systems (MSIS) program and the Master of Business Adminis-
tration (MBA) program at the University of Mary Hardin-Baylor during the Spring 2007
semester. The Kirton A-I Inventory [Kirton, 1976] found in Appendix A was distributed to
the students during a typical class period in the middle of their semester term.
r esults
A summary of the Kirton A-I scores is shown in Table C-2 through Table C-7 below.
c onclusion
Our research hypothesis is there are no differences in the problem solving styles between
college graduate students who are in the MSIS program and students who are in the MBA pro-
gram as measured by the Kirton A-I Inventory. Therefore, we compared the mean scores of the

students in the MSIS program and the students in the MBA program, as shown in Table C-2
below. Both groups of graduate students scored in the “mild innovator” category. This sup-
ports our hypothesis that there is no difference in their problem solving styles. However, the
sample size is too small to warrant a high confidence level and more research in this area is
needed.
Since earlier research indicated a difference in problem solving styles based on gender, we
included this demographic in Table C-2 below. However, the data did not suggest a differ-
ence in the overall score based solely on gender. Both male and female graduate students
scored at the “mild innovator” level.

An interesting difference emerges when the KAI scores are divided by the student’s undergrad-
uate academic major, as shown in Table C-4 and Table C-5 below. The students who scored at
the “mild adaptor” level had an undergraduate emphasis in accounting, computer information
systems, and computer science. The students who scored at the “medium innovator” level had
an undergraduate emphasis in management, computer graphics design, biology, and church
music. It seems logical to have accounting majors and computer science majors who are adap-
tors, which means they prefer a more structured environment. It seems equally consistent to
have management, computer graphics, biology, and music majors who are innovators, which

Another interesting outcome from this study is revealed when the KAI scores are divided
based on the number of years of work experience, as shown in Table C-6 below. The gradu-
ate students with less than 5 years of work experience scored at the “mild innovator” level.
Those students who have between 5 and 10 years of work experience scored in the “medium
innovator” level. Finally, those students with 15 or more years of work experience scored in
the “mild adaptor” level. Since prior research suggests a person’s KAI scores do not tend to
change over time, this data suggests that graduate students with less than 10 years of work
experience tend to be innovators, while graduate students with over 10 years of experience
tend to be adaptors. However, the sample size is too small to place a high level of confidence
in this area and more research is warranted in the relationship between the work experience
of graduate students and their KAI scores.

Kirton identified three “sub-factors” in the A-I Inventory questions. These three factors are
the sufficiency of originality (SO), efficiency (E), and rule conformity (R). We analyzed the
data according to these three sub-factors in Table C-7 below. The SO factor addresses
the difference people have when developing new ideas. Adaptors tend to produce fewer
ideas, which are also more sound and useful to the problem solving process. Innovators tend
to produce more ideas, with many of them being outside the box and more risky. The mean
SO score for the general population is 40.8 points and questions 1 through 12 on the KAI
measure a person’s SO factor. Our sample data did not indicate a difference in the SO factor
based on the graduate program or gender.

The rule conformity (R) sub-factor measures differences in people’s management structure
during the problem solving process. Adaptors tend to accept the rules and even view the
rules as an aid to the problem solving process. They also place more emphasis on group
cohesion. Innovators view rules and group cohesion as limitations on the problem solving
process. They often ignore the rules and pursue their own ideas. The mean R score for the
general population is 35.4 and questions 13 through 18 on the KAI measure a person’s R fac-
tor. Our sample data indicated a difference in the student’s R factor scores. Students in the
MBA program had higher R factor scores, which indicate they tend to follow the rules more
and value group cohesion. Students in the MSIS program had lower R factor scores, which
720 n n n A ppendix c
indicate they tend to ignore the rules and develop their own ideas. Our data also showed a
difference in the R factor scores based on gender. Our data suggests male students tend to
have a higher R factor score, which indicates they tend to follow the rules more and even
view rules as an aid. The female students in our sample had lower R factor scores, which
indicate they view rules and group cohesion as limits on the decision making process. More
research is warranted in the R sub-factor of graduate students based on our results.
The efficiency (E) sub-factor measures the attention people give to detail when solving
a problem. Adaptors tend to be more organized, arrange facts in an orderly method, and
search for information that is relevant to the problem in a logical manner. Innovators tend
to pay less attention to detail, are less thorough, and prefer to develop new ideas rather than
search for relevant information. The mean E score for the general population is 18.8 and
questions 19 through 32 on the KAI measure a person’s E factor. Our data did not indicate
any significant difference in the E factor among the graduate students, although students in
the MSIS program scored slightly higher than students in the MBA program. Also, female
students scored slightly higher than male students.

Hardin-Baylor. He received his B.S. in Business Administration from Clarion University
of Pennsylvania in 1982, his MBA from Oklahoma City University in 1989, and Ph.D. in
Economic Education from Ohio University in 1995. Dr. Stock teaches and conducts research

RONALD S. KING is a Professor of Business Information and Technology Systems at the

chunks.heading: PROJECT TEAM DYNAMICS
chunks.content:
PROJECT TEAM DYNAMICS
Ronald S. King
University of Mary Hardin-Baylor

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ABSTRACT
chunks.content:
ABSTRACT
Problem solving styles and interpersonal dynamics of project teams are often critical dimen-
sions of the ability of a team to function effectively. In order to study the problem solving
styles of students enrolled in a graduate Database Administration and Development class at
the University of Mary Hardin-Baylor (UMHB) and to track their intra-team interactions,
the theory established by M. J. Kirton in 1976, was used to determine the cognitive styles of
the students. The author categorized students according to Adaption-Innovation character-
istics by the Kirton AI Inventory. These categorizations were then applied to interpret the
results of interviews from informants, the team leaders, and about the abilities of project team
members to work and communicate with each other.
i ntroduction
Seven students were divided into one team of four students and one team of three students.
The teams were asked to design, implement, and evaluate a commercial application database
with a Web front-end. Each team leader had completed an undergraduate science degree
(one in computer science and the other in biology), had a high GMAT score, a graduate
GPA greater than 3.5, and at least seven years of professional experience in the information
systems field. Each team was assigned a student who completed an undergraduate computer
graphics design degree program, and each team was assigned one military personnel who is
currently enrolled in the MSIS program at UMHB. The goal of each project is to expose the
students to a simulated and significant corporate initiative that has both technological and
managerial dimensions, as well as to allow them to experience the conflicts and management
issues that can arise in an intensive team environment.
The Kirton KAI inventory, refer to Appendix B, was administered and each student was clas-
sified using the resultant scores. After interviewing the MSIS degree program director and
using the list of characteristics for an adaptor and an innovator for each member in the class,
the author qualitatively cross validated the classifications assigned to the students as either an
adaptor or an innovator. The director and the author have known every team member from
previous classes. Additionally, this is a degree program that requires each student applicant

The Kirton A-I Inventory total score can be broken down into three interrelated sub-scores.
Sufficiency of Originality (SO), Efficiency for Details (E), and Conformity to Norm Group
or Rule (R) are the sub-scores or factors [Kirton, M. J., 1994, 1998]. The SO sub-score
relates to a person’s style of idea generation, the E sub-score relates to one’s method of prob-
lem solving, and the R sub-score relates to a person’s style when dealing with structure, both
impersonal, in a group, and personal, or individually [Kirton, M. J., 1998].
The Sufficiency of Originality (SO) sub-factor deals with the difference people have in their
preferred handling of ideas. Adaptors prefer to produce fewer ideas when the consensus of
existing ideas is generally agreed upon in terms of soundness and usefulness. Thinking out of
the box and taking risks is perceived as valuable by innovators. Assuming a normal distribu-
tion of scores, over the sum of the items 1 through 12, implies that SO scores range from 12
to 60 with the general population mean of 36.
The Efficiency for Detail (E) sub-factor deals with the attention people give to detail when
problem solving or during decision making. Searching methodically and organizing data in
an orderly fashion are preferred methodologies of adaptors. On the other hand, innovators
pay less attention to details and prefer to initiate fresh and new approaches to problem
solving. Assuming a normal distribution of scores, over the sum of the items 13 through 18,
implies that the E scale ranges from 6 to 30 with the general population mean of 18.
[Kirton, M. J., 1994] explains that adaptors and innovators do not naturally work well together.
However, bringing together adaptors and innovators on the same team would benefit the
team by enabling them to consider a greater variety of alternatives during the problem solv-
ing process. As the difference between adaptor and innovator Kirton A-I Inventory perfor-
mance scores widen, then teamwork becomes more difficult [Kirton, M. J., 1998]. This latter
Appendix c n n n 725
fact is simply due to the natural tendency that people often prefer to work with others like
themselves. The Kirton A-I Inventory performance scores can make us aware of differences in
team members cognitive styles thus allowing for the accommodation of those style differences.

The Conformity to Group Norm or Rule (R) sub-factor describes differences in the manage-
ment structure within which problem-solving and decision making take place. Adaptors accept
rules as a structure within which to aid the efficiency of deriving solutions in problem-solving
while emphasizing group consensus and cohesion. Rather than play by the rules and seek
group approval, the innovators tend to break loose or ignore rules in their individual pursuit for
solutions. Again assuming a normal distribution of scores, over the sum of the items 19 through
33, implies that the R scales ranges from 15 to 75 with the general population mean of 45.
A study, utilizing the Kirton A-I Inventory, that compared the problem-solving style, in terms
of adaption and innovation, of Information and Computer Science majors was conducted by
[Sim, E. R. and Wright, G., 2002]. This study concluded that there is no difference in pro-
gramming styles between information systems and computer science students as measured
by the Kirton’s A-I Inventory. The study did conclude, however, there was a gender differ-
ence in the Kirton A-I Inventory scores; women scored slightly more adaptively then men.
[Kaufmann, G., Isaken, S. G., and Lauer, K., 1996] developed a regression plane showing the
distribution of Kirton A-I Inventory scores across managerial levels by gender. These authors
found a striking gender difference when observing Kirton A-I Inventory scores for males
and females analyzed across managerial levels. Males were found to be more innovatively
inclined than females at the lowest managerial level, whereas females obtained almost a full
standard deviation higher innovator score at the top, executive, level of leadership.

3. Methodical, prudent, rarely challenges rules except when fully supported

1. Proliferates ideas, however relevant they may seem
2. Thinks “outside the box;” interested in the “big picture”
3. Approaches tasks from unsuspected angles
4. Questions the basic assumptions, attempts to manipulate problems
5. Breaks from the mold; challenges rules
6. Prefers to work alone
